title: Annuity or Bond Ladder for Lifetime Income? Here’s How I Finally Chose.
summary: Compare an annuity and a bond ladder using a $100,000 example to see how each can build retirement income and help your nest egg last longer.
body_markdown:
[Retirement income](https://smartasset.com/retirement/average-retirement-income) can help cover living expenses once a paycheck stops, while adding another layer of flexibility to stretch your nest egg further. Two common strategies for building this income stream include annuities and bond ladders. However, you may need to prioritize one over the other for your retirement needs. Let’s break down an example to help you decide which can fit your lifetime income goals.


## Annuity vs. Bond Ladder: How Each May Build Retirement Income


Both[retirement income strategies](https://smartasset.com/retirement/7-types-of-retirement-income-sources) focus on creating predictable income streams and managing risk, but differ in how long the income can last and the level of control you have over your money.


An[annuity is an insurance contract](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-an-annuity) that could offer lifetime income in exchange for a lump sum or series of payments. Some contracts may cover a spouse’s lifetime too, but that choice can affect your payment amount. The terms depend on the contract, including when payments begin and what happens to any remaining value after the annuitant dies.


A[bond ladder,](https://smartasset.com/investing/how-to-make-a-bond-ladder) by comparison, is a portfolio of individual bonds with different maturity dates. A retiree might hold, for example, bonds that mature in successive years. The staggered schedule can make cash flows more predictable, but the income depends on the terms and issuers of the bond.


This table compares reasons for and against each strategy across four common retirement income goals:


Goals Reasons For Reasons Against


[Lifetime income](https://smartasset.com/retirement/payout-annuity) • **Annuity:** you want payments that may last for as long as you live.
• **Bond ladder:** you want predictable income for a set stretch of retirement. • **Annuity:** you are uneasy relying on an insurer’s ability to pay claims.
• **Bond ladder:** you want income that continues after the last bond matures.


[Access to your money](https://smartasset.com/investing/how-to-invest-cash) • **Annuity:** you are comfortable committing money for steady payments, and some contracts may allow limited withdrawals.
• **Bond ladder:** you want principal back as bonds mature, and bonds can generally be sold. • **Annuity:** you may need the money back and could face surrender charges or fees.
• **Bond ladder:** you may need to sell early and could take a loss if interest rates have risen.


[Keeping up with inflation](https://smartasset.com/investing/inflation-calculator) • **Annuity:** you want the option of payments that adjust for inflation.
• **Bond ladder:** you want to reinvest maturing principal at current rates or hold inflation-linked bonds. • **Annuity:** inflation adjustments generally lower the starting payment.
• **Bond ladder:** reinvesting at lower rates can reduce your income.


[Leaving money to heirs](https://smartasset.com/investing/how-does-inheritance-work) • **Annuity:** you want a death benefit or guaranteed payment period for beneficiaries.
• **Bond ladder:** you want remaining bonds to pass to heirs. • **Annuity:** a payout that ends at death may leave nothing.
• **Bond ladder:** what heirs receive depends on how much you spend and on bond values.


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_annuities&utm_content=annuityorbondladderforlifetimeincomehereishowichose_a) can help you determine how much of your essential expenses a guaranteed income source could cover.**


## Annuity vs. Bond Ladder: What $100,000 Might Do for Your Nest Egg


To see how each strategy can impact your retirement plan, let’s assume that you are 65 years old and have set aside $100,000 to generate income. First, you consider taking an[immediate annuity](https://smartasset.com/retirement/immediate-annuity) , which pays about $7,000 annually for life based on a 7% annual rate. Then you compare it with a bond ladder that has 10 rungs maturing over a decade at an average 4% yield. The table calculates the totals:


Amounts Immediate Annuity Bond Ladder


Retirement income investment $100,000 $100,000


Annual income $100,000 × 7% = $7,000 $100,000 × 4% ÷ (1 − 1.04^−10) = $12,329


How long the income lasts For life 10 years


Total received by age 75 $7,000 × 10 = $70,000 $12,329.09 × 10 = $123,291


Total received by age 85 $7,000 × 20 = $140,000 $123,291 (income has ended)


Total received by age 95 $7,000 × 30 = $210,000 $123,291 (income has ended)


Year annuity passes ladder Year 18: $7,000 × 18 = $126,000 Year 17: $119,000 vs. $123,291


Both examples invest the full $100,000 and exclude inflation, taxes and fees. The annuity pays a flat $7,000 annually for as long as you live, while the ladder spreads the money across 10 bonds that mature one year apart. You spend each year’s interest and maturing principal until the last bond is gone.


Amounts will vary based on the size of your annuity payout, your age, the insurer and[interest rates](https://smartasset.com/investing/bond-yield-vs-interest-rate) . Income from a bond ladder will also depend on available yields and the bonds you choose. Both investments can lose money, since an annuity’s guarantee depends on the insurer’s ability to pay claims, and a ladder can lose value if you sell a bond early or an issuer fails to pay.


When comparing estimates, the table show how an annuity can pay more than twice the original investment in 30 years ($210,000). A bond ladder with the same $100,000 investment will pay almost twice as much as the annuity in the first 10 years ($123,291).


## How You Can Decide Between an Annuity and a Bond Ladder


If your biggest[concern is outliving your savings](https://smartasset.com/retirement/running-out-of-money-in-retirement) , then an annuity can offer lifetime payments. A bond ladder, on the other hand, would only cover a specific number of years. It does, however, offer more access to your money, since you may sell a bond early if you need cash.[Reinvesting in another ladder](https://smartasset.com/investing/bond-laddering-strategies) after bond maturity could also help your income keep up with inflation and might even outpace annuity payments over time.


As another alternative, your plan may combine the guaranteed income of an annuity with the flexibility of a ladder. For example, you can buy an annuity to cover housing, food and insurance, while a ladder holds your money for future expenses and could be reinvested as bonds mature. To see how much guaranteed income you might want, add up what you must pay each month and subtract the income you already expect from[other sources like Social Security](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-calculator) .


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_annuities&utm_content=annuityorbondladderforlifetimeincomehereishowichose_a) can help you decide how much to put in an annuity or a bond ladder, and recommend other strategies.**
